title: Research Bite #75: Germane Processes Moderate the Effectiveness of Complex Desirable Difficulty Tasks (tipsforteachers.substack.com), September 7, 2026
author: Craig Barton
source: Tips for Teachers, discussing Zeitlhofer & Zumbach, Instructional Science
summary: Craig Barton's Research Bites series breaks down a 2026 Instructional Science paper by Ines Zeitlhofer and Joerg Zumbach that directly tests two education theories often assumed to give conflicting advice: cognitive load theory (which suggests raising task complexity gradually) and desirable difficulty theory (which suggests making practice harder from the start, including by interleaving rather than blocking topics). In a 2x2 factorial study, 132 Austrian adults learned to conjugate an unfamiliar Italian verb across six tenses under one of four combinations of complexity and interleaving, and were tested two days later; the group that practiced at full complexity from the start, with topics shuffled rather than blocked, solved the delayed test fastest and with the fewest attempts, while the easiest, most blocked condition performed worst. Critically, the paper's own abstract reports that interest and self-reported confidence were no lower in the harder conditions, directly undercutting the common worry that raising difficulty will demoralize students, and frames cognitive load itself as a driver of the metacognitive engagement that produced the performance gains rather than simply an obstacle to avoid. Barton is careful to flag the study's limits for classroom transfer -- adult volunteers, a single one-hour session, one narrow language-learning domain, and performance measured as speed and attempt-count rather than accuracy -- while still drawing the concrete instructional implication that if a class already has the prerequisite knowledge, giving them the full-difficulty, interleaved version of a task from the outset may outperform the conventional practice of gradually scaffolding up to it.
points: The study directly pits cognitive load theory's 'start easy, build up' instinct against desirable difficulty theory's 'go hard from the start,' finding the full-complexity, interleaved condition beat gradual buildup and blocked practice on a test given two days later -- not immediately, which is the more common and less durable measure teachers usually see.

Interest and self-reported confidence were statistically unaffected by task difficulty, directly undercutting the common teacher assumption that harder tasks from the outset will demoralize students or damage their willingness to engage.

The paper's own framing treats cognitive load not purely as an obstacle to minimize but as a driver of the metacognitive engagement that produced the performance benefit -- the difficulty itself is doing productive work, not merely being tolerated.

Barton's caution list is as load-bearing as the finding itself: adult volunteers, a single one-hour lab session, one narrow language domain, and a performance measure of speed/attempts rather than accuracy all limit how directly this can be extrapolated to a K-12 classroom, and the authors themselves describe it as one experiment in one domain.
quotes: This Austrian experiment tested both at once. 132 adults with no Italian spent an hour learning to conjugate one Italian verb across six tenses and modal forms, randomly assigned to one of four versions of the task.

Those who had worked at constantly high complexity, and those whose practice was interleaved, solved it faster and with fewer attempts. The hardest combination did best, and the easiest did worst. Interest and confidence were unaffected.

The authors report that "confronting learners with complex desirable difficulty tasks was effective in fostering performance," and that "cognitive load was revealed as one of the major reasons for learners' metacognitive engagement.

The group that had been at full difficulty all along completed the delayed test faster and with fewer attempts. If your class already has the prerequisites, consider giving them the whole version of the task from the outset rather than building up to it in stages.

These learners were given the full table of verb endings to refer to, got immediate right-or-wrong feedback on every attempt, and moved on automatically after a minute. The authors are explicit that this only works when learners have enough prior knowledge to have a proper attempt at the task.
Findings of the present study suggest that manipulating tasks in a way that allows them to be easily solved might underestimate a learner's cognitive potential.
